notes.body:
The supplication of drawing near (دُعَاءُ التَّقَرُّبِ) is a **specific, named liturgical prayer** — a known text with a known purpose — that Ismaili worshippers recite after the daily obligatory prayers. The chapter assumes familiarity with it the way a teacher assumes a student already knows what "the opening chapter" means; every practitioner recognizes it.

The seven types that follow are categories based on **posture and gesture** — each defined not by what is said but by how the body is held:

- asking (دُعَاءُ الْمَسْأَلَةِ) — palms facing the worshipper
- seeking refuge (دُعَاءُ الْاِسْتِعَاذَةِ) — palms turned away
- humble submission (دُعَاءُ الْاِسْتِكَانَةِ) — hands grasping the shoulders
- devotion (دُعَاءُ التَّبَتُّلِ) — the index finger raised
- entreaty (دُعَاءُ التَّضَرُّعِ) — the finger moving
- fervent appeal (دُعَاءُ الْاِبْتِهَالِ) — both arms extended skyward
- abasement in the dust (دُعَاءُ التَّعْفِيرِ) — cheeks pressed to the ground

Not one of these is defined by a particular text or topic — they are modes, not prayers.

Imagine someone asks: "Should we sing our national anthem tonight, or any song at all?" The national anthem is **a specific, cherished text with its own identity**; "a song" is a broad category. The supplication of drawing near (دُعَاءُ التَّقَرُّبِ) is like the national anthem; the seven types are like musical genres — hymn, lament, march — that describe how any song might be performed.

The questioner wonders whether the ruling — that supplication is discouraged after the afternoon prayer — applies only to this one well-known prayer, or to **every form of supplication** altogether. The answer is that it covers all supplications, not only this specific one, and that no sin falls on whoever does supplicate.

The supplication of drawing near (دُعَاءُ التَّقَرُّبِ) is not missing from the list of seven — it was never meant to appear there. The seven types are a taxonomy of form; دُعَاءُ التَّقَرُّبِ is a specific act of worship. One could recite it with palms spread wide in the mode of fervent appeal, or with the index finger raised in the mode of devotion — the two frameworks describe **different dimensions** of the same practice.
notes.anchor: the supplication of drawing near, or all supplications
notes.quote: the supplication of drawing near, or all supplications
etymology: دُعَاءُ (supplication): from the root د-ع-و, meaning to call or to summon. دَعَا means to call out toward someone; the noun دُعَاءُ is the act of that calling. Every supplication is therefore a cry directed upward — a voice naming what the heart most deeply needs, cast across the distance between us and Allah.

التَّقَرُّبِ (drawing near): from the root ق-ر-ب, meaning to be close. The verb قَرُبَ means to come near; the reflexive form تَقَرَّبَ means to bring oneself near — to actively close the distance between the soul and its source. This supplication is not merely a request; it is a movement of the whole self toward Allah.

الْاِبْتِهَالِ (fervent appeal): from the root ب-ه-ل, meaning to be free and unrestrained — to pour oneself out without holding anything back. The form اِبْتِهَالٌ carries this sense of total release, which is why this mode calls for both palms spread wide and both arms raised high: the body itself becomes the expression of an open heart.

التَّعْفِيرِ (abasement in the dust): from the root ع-ف-ر, referring to dust or the bare surface of the earth (عَفَر). To perform تَعْفِيرٌ is to press one's cheek into that earth — not as degradation, but as the soul's acknowledgment that before Allah all pretension dissolves, and all distance collapses.

notes.body:
The paradox is only on the surface. The word مبرم carries the image of a rope twisted and braided until it cannot be undone. So when Maulana Ali says that supplication (الدعاء) reverses even this, he is not describing a loophole in the divine order. He is pointing to a **mechanism woven into creation itself**.

The twelve foundations of supplication make that mechanism visible. Before any petition is voiced, the believer repents, gives charity, fasts or prays, purifies the heart — and then, most critically, draws near through the Imams of the religion, naming them one by one until reaching the living Imam of the age. A supplication built this way is no longer the cry of an isolated, unchanged self; it is a soul that has passed through the living chain of divine guidance and **reached the level where decrees originate**.

The Quran names this movement:

إِلَيْهِ يَصْعَدُ ٱلْكَلِمُ ٱلطَّيِّبُ وَٱلْعَمَلُ ٱلصَّلِحُ يَرْفَعُهُ
To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it.

Fatir 35:10

It is righteous action that **carries the word upward** — which is precisely what Maulana Ali means when he says the one who supplicates without deeds is like an archer with no bowstring. The arrow is the petition; the string is the transformed life behind it.

The deepest point is this: the decree was sealed upon a soul in a specific state — heedless, distant, unchanged. **The transformed soul** that emerges from the twelve foundations is no longer that person, and the seal no longer fits the new shape of the self. Because Allah's knowledge already contained this moment of turning, the reversal was always part of the divine order, not a breach of it.
notes.anchor: Supplication turns back the decree that has been firmly settled
notes.quote: Supplication turns back the decree that has been firmly settled
etymology: القضاء (decree): from the root ق-ض-ي, meaning to complete, to settle, or to execute to the end. What has been قُضِيَ is cut through and finalised — the root carries the image of a thing driven to its conclusion with no thread left hanging. The word serves for both 'decree' and 'judgment' because in divine speech the two are a single act.

مبرم (firmly settled): from the root ب-ر-م, meaning to twist or braid tightly. A cord that has been أُبْرِمَ is wound so fast it resists loosening. The word is tactile — you feel the grip of it. That is precisely what makes Maulana Ali's teaching so charged: even the braided rope of fate yields to sincere supplication.

الدعاء (supplication): from the root د-ع-و, meaning to call out or to summon. The same root gives دعا — he called. Supplication is not a silent petition; it is a voice launched across the distance between creature and Creator, naming what is needed and trusting it will be heard and answered.
